title: Sleep wearables
text: Sleep posture analysis with intelligent wearable sensing.

title: Sleep wearables
section: 1 What draws me to this area
text:
1 What draws me to this area
I am interested in how wearable technologies can help us understand body posture and movement during sleep. This area brings together several things that motivate my research: developing sensing systems, understanding human biomechanics, and turning measurements into information that clinicians and lay users can interpret and act upon.
Beyond recognising an individual posture, I am interested in the patterns that emerge over time: how positions change, how long they are maintained, and what we can learn from the relationship between in-bed posture/movement and other physiological phenomena.

title: Sleep wearables
text:
2 Questions that interest me
Some of the questions I explore include:

How much can we learn about body posture from a finite set of biomechanical and sensor measurements?
How can we recognise different postures when collecting large labelled datasets is difficult?
How can we describe posture changes and periods of inactivity in an understandable way?

These questions also open opportunities to connect wearable sensing with wider interests in biomechanics, human movement and healthcare engineering.

title: Sleep wearables
text:
3 Bringing sensing and interpretation together
My work combines bespoke wearable sensor development, measurements of joint orientation and movement, and computational methods for recognising patterns. I am particularly interested in representations that connect sensor measurements to the biophysical quantities they describe.
Rather than treating sensing and analysis as separate tasks, I explore how the choice of measurements and the methods used to interpret them can work together to provide useful information about posture and movement.

title: Sleep wearables
text:
4 Contributions from my work
Working with collaborators, I have explored how complex sleep postures can be recognised from joint-angle information using very limited labelled training data. Our one-shot learning framework examined twelve non-standard postures through computer-generated data and a human-participant pilot study, bringing together wearable sensing, sensor fusion and kinematic data augmentation. Read the posture-learning paper.
A complementary strand of work examines when posture changes occur and how periods of postural inactivity can be described. We developed an interpretable framework using wrist kinematics, evaluated in a controlled study with five healthy participants during simulated sleep. This connects posture recognition with an understanding of movement over time. Read the posture-change and inactivity paper.
Together, these studies contribute methods for analysing sleep-related posture and movement, while providing a foundation for further investigation in varied contexts.

title: Sleep wearables
text:
5 Possibilities and connections
I am interested in extending this work towards sensing approaches that are practical, adaptable and informative beyond controlled experiments. Possible directions include understanding differences between individuals, learning with limited examples, and exploring how movement information could support broader biomechanics and healthcare research.
I would welcome conversations with researchers, clinicians and prospective research students who share these interests—or who bring complementary ideas. There is room for contributions spanning sensor development, intelligent algorithms, experimental biomechanics and the interpretation of human movement.
Get in touch (elnaggar.omar at outlook dot com).

title: Educational technology
section: 1 What draws me to this area
text:
1 What draws me to this area
I am interested in how students develop an understanding of engineering: how they connect theory with the behaviour of real systems, learn through experimentation, and develop confidence in their own judgement. My work explores the design of assessments and digital resources to support that process.
My experience teaching robotics, mechatronics, control and engineering computing has made these connections especially important to me. An equation becomes more meaningful when students can change a parameter, observe what happens and explain why. Equally, building a working system creates opportunities to question assumptions, interpret imperfect measurements and learn from unexpected behaviour.
I want to create learning experiences that give students room to investigate, discuss and make decisions, while helping educators quantify, understand and support that learning.

title: Educational technology
text:
2 Questions that interest me
Some questions that motivate my work include:

How can interactive activities help students ground engineering theory in practice?
How can virtual and physical laboratories complement one another?
How can we quantify and interpret within-class knowledge exchange in collaborative activities?
How can educators create useful, accessible interactive teaching materials?

These are starting points for exploration. Different engineering subjects, student backgrounds and teaching contexts bring further questions of their own.

title: Educational technology
text:
3 Learning through experimentation
I am interested in practical learning that gives students meaningful choices: forming a prediction, testing an idea, comparing observations and revising an explanation. Physical laboratories, design-build activities and virtual experiments offer different opportunities for this kind of exploration.
Working with collaborators, I have developed game-based virtual engineering laboratories, including work presented through mechanical and computer engineering case studies at the Advance HE Teaching and Learning Conference in 2022. I also served as technology lead and co-investigator on the Studentainment virtual-laboratory project.
For me, the interesting challenge is connecting the activity with what students need to understand. I would like to explore how virtual environments can support preparation, repeated experimentation and reflection alongside the practical experience of working with physical equipment.

title: Educational technology
text:
4 Making engineering concepts interactive
Interactive resources can let students explore relationships that are difficult to communicate through a static diagram alone. In my teaching materials, I use controls and visual feedback to invite students to change a system’s parameters and examine its response. Robot control provides one example of this approach.
With Roselina Arelhi, I presented a framework for creating interactive learning materials with generative AI at Advance HE in 2025. This work explores how educators can develop and customise resources without extensive technical expertise.
I am interested in making this process more approachable while keeping educators’ judgement central: checking technical accuracy, choosing useful interactions and considering how different students will access and use the material.


Watch an example: exploring robot control








A recorded demonstration of my interactive robot-control teaching material. It shows parameter controls alongside visual feedback about system behaviour.

title: Educational technology
text:
5 Understanding learning and collaboration
Engineering work depends on explaining ideas, interpreting someone else’s work and contributing to shared decisions. I am interested in learning activities that make those processes visible, and in evidence that helps educators understand students’ developing knowledge.
In our 2021 classroom knowledge-exchange study, Roselina Arelhi and I explored a group-coursework framework involving a handover between teams. We combined survey information with AI-based visualisation to investigate students’ knowledge alongside conventional assessment measures.
This experience informs my interest in authentic assessment, constructive feedback and collaborative learning. More recently, I have contributed to a departmental, evidence-led demonstrator-training development at Queen Mary’s School of Engineering and Materials Science. Across these activities, I want to understand both the learning experience and the support students need to participate effectively.

title: Educational technology
text:
6 Possibilities and connections
I would like to explore further connections between practical engineering education, interactive resources and the evaluation of learning. Possible directions include linking virtual and physical experiments, developing resources with students and educators, and examining how different learners engage with collaborative activities.
I welcome conversations with engineering educators, education researchers, developers and prospective research students. If you are interested in laboratory learning, interactive engineering concepts, knowledge exchange or thoughtful uses of AI in education, I would be pleased to hear from you.
Get in touch (elnaggar.omar at outlook dot com).

title: Omar Elnaggar
text:
What I Do
Robotics and automation teaching
I help undergraduate and postgraduate students turn engineering theory into working systems. My teaching spans robotics, mechatronics, control, artificial intelligence and engineering computing, using authentic practical laboratories, design-build activities and project supervision to develop technical skills, critical thinking and professional judgement. At UCL, I contribute to Robotics for Medicine and Industry, teaching prosthetics, wearable technologies and biomechanics.
Wearable sensing and biomechanics research
I develop and evaluate methods to understand human posture and movement, combining wearable sensors, machine learning, experimental measurements and computational modelling. My doctoral research focused on intelligent wearable sensing for sleep posture assessment. My subsequent research experience includes clinical gait analysis and the biomechanics of ageing foot tissues, working with engineers and clinicians to connect engineering methods with healthcare questions.
Engineering education
I design and investigate practical, active learning experiences that help students understand complex engineering concepts and apply them with confidence. My educational research and development includes virtual engineering laboratories, game-based learning and AI-supported interactive materials. I combine these approaches with authentic assessment, inclusive teaching and constructive feedback to support students’ participation and development.

title: Omar Elnaggar
text:
Technical Skills
Robotics, sensing and embedded systems
Wearable sensor development, embedded C/C++, PCB design, microcontroller-based prototyping, sensor fusion, digital signal processing and feedback control. Experience with the Robot Operating System (ROS) and programmable logic controllers (PLCs).
Programming, machine learning and data analysis
Python and MATLAB/Simulink for engineering computation, signal analysis and algorithm development; machine learning and deep learning using TensorFlow and PyTorch, alongside data visualisation and interpretable approaches to sensor-based analysis.
Human movement measurement and biomedical imaging
Optical and wearable motion capture, including Vicon, OptiTrack, Qualisys and inertial sensors; force-plate and plantar-pressure measurements; ultrasound, MRI and biplanar X-ray imaging. Experimental data acquisition, preprocessing and validation against reference measurements.
Computational biomechanics
Musculoskeletal modelling and inverse kinematic and dynamic analysis with OpenSim; medical image segmentation with 3D Slicer and Avizo; subject-specific finite-element modelling and tissue analysis using Abaqus.
Educational technology and interactive development
Virtual engineering laboratories, game-based resources and AI-supported interactive learning materials. HTML/CSS, 3D modelling and animation, with experience using Moodle, Blackboard and Canvas to support teaching and learning.

title: What stayed with me from India
text:
I went to India to study feet, footwear and ageing gait. What I keep coming back to is the way people welcomed us.
In January 2025, our biomechanics research took us to Bangalore and rural communities in Karnataka. We brought a portable experimental setup distributed across several bags and suitcases, found places to work, and collected unique and valuable field measurements from volunteers. That is the straightforward version of the trip. It leaves out almost everything that made it special.



Fieldwork in Karnataka, January 2025. Photograph: Dr Kristiaan (Kris) D’Août.


At one of the rural sites, we set up in a local school. People who had never met us welcomed us warmly, even when we didn’t share a language. There was something quite moving about that: arriving as a stranger and being made to feel welcome before you had much chance to explain yourself.
Dozens of people came to take part. They waited in a queue, sometimes for a long time, until we were ready for them. I remember concentrating on the feet I was scanning and noticing traces of mud nestled deep in the folds and grooves that years of hard work had etched into their skin. To me, these muddy traces tell their own story, honouring the lives and hard work of the people who stood before me.
That detail has stayed with me. We were measuring feet that carried people through lives we knew very little about. For a short time, those lives crossed with ours, and people gave us their time and trusted us to do our work.
It made the word “participant” feel rather small.
Then, after all that, there was food.
Members of the community had cooked for us in a modest kitchen-like space without much lighting. I hadn’t expected it. They had already welcomed us, helped make the work possible, and waited patiently while we collected our measurements. Somewhere in the middle of that, someone had also decided that we should be fed.
The food tasted as warm as the welcome.
I remember that feeling from so many of the rural places we visited: how difficult it seemed to leave without somebody offering us something home-cooked. I was conscious of the resources people were working with, which made their generosity especially touching. But what I remember most is how naturally they offered it. We were their guests, and they made sure we felt it.



A view along the way in Karnataka.


The school gave me another memory I still return to. Kris stepped into a classroom and greeted the students. Daylight came through the window, and the pupils were extraordinarily attentive and disciplined, perhaps the most disciplined I have ever seen.
I wouldn’t pretend that a brief visit told me everything about their education or their lives. Still, the seriousness with which those students approached learning made an impression on me, as did the commitment of the teachers working with them. Resources were limited. The desire to learn was very much there.
It made me think about my own education, and about how easily something that once felt like an opportunity can become an expectation. Access to equipment, a comfortable place to work, the simple assumption that the things you need will be available: I had grown used to a great deal.
I came home more grateful for those things, and a little less comfortable taking them for granted.
Some of the most personal moments happened at the end of the measurements. Elderly participants would sometimes tap my shoulder after I had finished working with their feet. I received those gestures as blessings, although I couldn’t be certain I understood their full meaning.
I found them deeply touching. I had been focused on getting the measurements right, being careful, and completing the work. Then a small gesture would draw me out of that concentration and remind me of the person sharing that moment with me.
I still think about it.
Having Dr Kristiaan (Kris) D’Août alongside me made the trip especially enjoyable. His network of collaborators in Bangalore helped make the work possible, and travelling with him brought another pleasure: the company of someone so open to exploring the world.
I appreciated that mindset. Being curious about a place, making room for unfamiliar ways of doing things, and enjoying what you encounter along the way can change the whole experience of travelling. I feel fortunate to have shared this one with him, and grateful to the local collaborators whose relationships and work allowed us to be there.
We also happened to be in India during the Maha Kumbh Mela, an extraordinary spiritual gathering held in Prayagraj every twelve years, with the 2025 celebration considered especially significant because of a rare celestial alignment said to occur only once in 144 years. Hundreds of millions of pilgrim visits were recorded during the festival that year. I didn’t attend the gathering myself, but simply being in the country while something of such immense scale and spiritual significance was taking place added another sense of wonder to the trip. There was so much happening beyond the small part of India I was getting to know. It made me want to understand more, while reminding me how much I had yet to understand.
Since coming home, I’ve found myself thinking more carefully about who my research is for.
I still care about the technical questions: how feet work, how tissues respond to load, how we measure movement well. But I’m increasingly interested in where those questions lead, whose experiences help shape them, and who might eventually benefit from the answers.
Working in Karnataka made those questions personal. It gave me the privilege of doing biomechanics research with communities whose everyday lives may be far removed from the settings in which much of our evidence is collected. It also made me want to look more closely at whose lives our findings can reasonably speak for, and whose we still need to understand.
I want that curiosity to influence the research I pursue: the people I work with, the places I go, and the practical value of what we develop together.
I don’t yet have a neat answer to what giving back should look like. That is something I want to work out with communities and local collaborators, by listening to what matters to them. But I know I want it to continue to be part of a meaningful biomechanics research journey.
When I think of that school now, I remember the equipment we brought and the measurements we collected. I also remember the queue, the classroom, the food, and the people who made room for us.
They had never met us before. They welcomed us anyway.
I hope I carry some of that generosity into whatever comes next.

title: Movement and tissue biomechanics
text: Field-based gait measurements in South India, showing wearable instrumentation and comparisons across footwear and surface conditions. Source: Evolutionary Morphology and Biomechanics Group, University of Liverpool.

title: Movement and tissue biomechanics
section: 1 What draws me to this area
text:
1 What draws me to this area
I am interested in how we move and the tissues that are involved in movement. Walking and balance bring this connection into focus: whole-body movement depends on the interaction of joints, muscles, soft tissues and the ground beneath our feet.
My research experience spans clinical human-motion analysis at Cambridge and foot and ankle biomechanics at Liverpool. Together, these experiences have shaped my interest in studying movement at different scales, from head and whole-body motion capture to the structure and mechanical behaviour of individual tissues. I bring sensing, biomedical imaging and computational modelling together to explore those connections.

title: Movement and tissue biomechanics
text:
2 Questions that interest me
Some questions that motivate my work include:

What can changes in walking and balance tell us, and how can we measure them reliably outside the laboratory?
How do tissue structure, ageing and loading interact with the mechanics of movement?
How can imaging and personalised models help us interpret differences between people?

These questions offer starting points for collaboration across engineering, biomechanics and clinically motivated research.

title: Movement and tissue biomechanics
section: 3 Understanding movement in a clinical context
text:
3 Understanding movement in a clinical context
At the University of Cambridge, I worked on head and whole-body movement analysis with medical consultants and clinical scientists at Addenbrooke’s Hospital (Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust). I contributed to the development of data processing pipelines for ear-based wearable devices for monitoring walking and activities of daily living, and planned optical motion-capture setups that are clinically relevant in the context of balance and neurological disorders.
A recurring question for me is what a measurement actually tells us: which features of movement are informative, how reliably they can be obtained, and how we can interpret them in relation to the person being assessed.

title: Movement and tissue biomechanics
text:
4 Looking beneath the surface
Ultrasound (US), bi-planar X-ray and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are important parts of my experience in biomechanics research. They offer complementary views of tissue structure, deformation and bone motion, helping connect external measurements with what happens within the body.
At Liverpool, I developed equipment for heel-pad ultrasound imaging and plantar-surface strain measurements. I also constructed participant-specific finite-element models from segmented foot MRI scans and conducted bi-planar X-ray videography experiments with simultaneous force-plate measurements to inform hindfoot simulations.
What draws me to this work is the possibility of linking anatomy with function. Ultrasound can reveal how the layers beneath the heel respond to loading; MRI provides anatomical information for personalised models; and bi-planar X-ray enables simultaneous investigation of motion and tissue behaviour. These approaches help explore mechanisms that are difficult to observe from the outside alone.







Ultrasound reveals the layered structure of the heel pad under load, including the skin, micro-chamber and macro-chamber layers above the calcaneus. From my ISB 2025 poster.

title: Movement and tissue biomechanics
text:
5 Contributions from my work
Working with colleagues at Liverpool, I contributed to participant studies in the UK, India and Namibia, combining tissue measurements, gait biomechanics and biomedical imaging. Our work included examining age-related differences in the layers of the heel pad. I also investigated spatiotemporal gait parameters across the three populations using both laboratory and field gait measurements, and their correlations with age, weight and other confounding variables.
I also explored a complementary question: can a quick measurement of surface hardness represent how heel tissues compress under load? Our conference work found that it did not reliably do so under the tested conditions. This illustrates a question I find especially important: when does a convenient measurement capture the behaviour we want to understand?
Alongside experimental work, I contributed to a critical review of footwear and locomotor health across the life course, examining the evidence behind common footwear features and their interaction with the foot’s own mechanics.

title: Movement and tissue biomechanics
text:
6 Connecting measurements and models
My approach combines wearable and optical sensing, force and pressure measurements, biomedical imaging, and musculoskeletal and finite-element modelling. I value their complementary perspectives: measurements describe movement and loading, imaging reveals anatomical structure, and models help investigate mechanical behaviour.
Across these activities, I aim to keep the analysis grounded in experimental evidence and attentive to variation between people.







From MRI segmentation to tissue modelling: anatomical segmentation, a three-dimensional mesh, applied boundary conditions and a finite-element analysis example. Selected panel from my research-methods portfolio, showing the connection between medical imaging and computational biomechanics.

title: Movement and tissue biomechanics
text:
7 Possibilities and connections
I would like to explore further connections between tissue biomechanics, whole-body movement and practical mobility assessment. Possible directions include combining wearable measurements with personalised models, studying variation across populations, and developing accessible ways to interpret biomechanical data.
I welcome conversations with researchers, clinicians and prospective research students interested in human movement, tissue mechanics, biomedical imaging or computational modelling. If your interests connect with these themes or bring a different perspective, I would be happy to hear from you.
Get in touch (elnaggar.omar at outlook dot com).
